questions.q: What is a Spot Instance (AWS) or Spot VM (Azure), fundamentally?
options: A dedicated, guaranteed GPU instance billed at a premium rate for mission-critical workloads
Spare cloud GPU capacity sold at a lower price, which the provider can reclaim with short notice
A free tier of GPU access offered only to new cloud accounts
A GPU instance type that physically cannot be interrupted once a job starts
questions.explain: Both clouds sell unused, spare capacity at a discount under the condition that it can be reclaimed on short notice when on-demand/reserved demand needs it, or (on Azure) when the spot price exceeds your max price.

questions.q: On AWS, roughly how much warning does EC2 give before reclaiming a Spot Instance?
options: No warning at all; the instance is terminated without any notice
Exactly 24 hours of advance notice in every case
One full week, matching the standard billing cycle
A commonly cited interruption notice on the order of about two minutes before reclamation
questions.explain: AWS delivers a short interruption notice, commonly around two minutes, before reclaiming a Spot Instance - not instantaneous, but far too short to manually save multi-hour training progress without automation.

questions.q: Why is losing a spot GPU instance mid-training a much bigger problem than losing a spot CPU instance mid-batch-job?
options: GPU instances cannot be relaunched once interrupted, while CPU instances can always be restarted
Spot CPU instances are never actually interrupted in practice
Training runs accumulate expensive, hours-long GPU compute as unsaved state; losing that state means redoing hours of work at the GPU's high rate, not just restarting a cheap batch job
CPU batch jobs are billed at the same rate as GPU training jobs, so there is no cost difference
questions.explain: A stateless CPU batch job loses only a few minutes of cheap, easily-redone work on interruption. A training job accumulates hours of expensive GPU compute in unsaved model/optimizer state, so losing it without a checkpoint means starting over from nothing.

questions.q: What specific practice from this course turns spot GPUs into a reasonable cost-optimization tool for training rather than a gamble?
options: Checkpointing model and optimizer state to durable storage at a reasonable interval, combined with automatic resume on new capacity after an interruption
Always running training jobs on exactly one GPU to minimize risk
Disabling spot pricing entirely and paying on-demand for every training job
Running every job twice simultaneously on two different spot instances
questions.explain: Checkpointing (covered in Chapter 3) means a spot interruption only costs the work done since the last checkpoint. Paired with a resumable job design, this is what makes the spot discount worth taking on training workloads.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say spot GPUs are generally a poor fit for real-time inference serving?
options: Inference workloads never run on GPUs, only on CPUs
Real-time serving workloads cannot tolerate an unscheduled eviction the way a checkpointed training job can - an interruption there means dropped requests, not a delayed training step
Spot pricing is not available for inference workloads on any cloud
Real-time serving is always cheaper than training, so the discount provides no benefit
questions.explain: Serving workloads generally need continuously available capacity with no tolerance for a gap; an eviction causes dropped requests immediately, unlike a checkpointed training job that can simply resume from its last saved state.
